Code editing to fix bugs in Python sourc: Use check_python_file_by_test_suite pattern: retrieve modified source files from VM, run a downloaded test suite against them by dynamically loading the test module and calling its test() function, returning a float score.

When verifying multi-file Python projects, ensure all related source files are fetched together and placed in the same working directory before running tests, since modules import each other by relative name.

The test suite is fetched from a cloud URL and executed in the same directory as the source files; sys.path and sys.modules must be cleaned up between evaluations to prevent module cache contamination across tasks.
Return value from the test function can be bool, int, or float; normalize to 0.0–1.0 range for scoring.

Use a downloaded test suite (check_python_file_by_test_suite pattern) that imports the edited source files and runs functional assertions; the metric loads files via importlib, so ensure module-level side effects (e.g., pygame.init) are guarded or mocked in the test suite
When verifying multi-file Python projects, the evaluator changes cwd to the test file's directory and inserts it into sys.path, so relative imports among project files must remain intact after edits
The metric normalizes return values: bool True→1.0, numeric clamped to [0,1], truthy non-numeric→1.0; write test functions that return a float proportion of passing sub-checks for partial credit
sys.modules cleanup is performed after each evaluation run to prevent module cache contamination across sequential tasks; avoid relying on cached module state between evaluator calls
Writing Python scripts for image process: Use SSIM (skimage.metrics.structural_similarity) with channel_axis=2 to compare output images against a reference; resize mismatched dimensions before comparison rather than failing outright

When verifying script-generated image output, check both that the output file exists and that its visual content matches a gold reference using structural similarity metrics rather than exact pixel equality

For image extraction/cropping scripts, verify the output image mode (e.g., RGBA for transparency) and that non-background regions are preserved correctly by comparing against a reference with a tolerance threshold around 0.85
Verify output image dimensions using PIL Image.open; check width and height attributes directly; optionally use getbbox on alpha channel when ignore_transparent is needed.
VS Code extension installation: Use `code --list-extensions` shell command output to verify an extension is installed; check for the extension's publisher.name identifier string using a contains check.
Writing Python scripts for data analysis: When the output is a numeric result file, compare as float with a small tolerance (e.g., 1e-4); also accept cases where the expected number appears as a substring of the actual content (e.g., result prefixed with a natural-language description).
Use compare_result_files-style logic: strip whitespace, attempt float conversion for numeric comparison, fall back to exact string equality for non-numeric content.

For median/statistical computation tasks, verify the script handles missing/empty values by imputing with the column mean before computing the statistic, and that the final scalar is written to the output file.
Writing Python scripts for file merging: Use python-docx's Document and paragraph APIs to compare paragraph text content between result and reference .docx files; the compare_docx_files metric normalizes whitespace and compares joined paragraph text, so focus on content equality rather than exact paragraph boundaries.

Font size in .docx is stored per-run (run.font.size) and per-paragraph style; when verifying document-wide font size, iterate over all runs across all paragraphs and check the size attribute (in Pt units).

When merging text files into a docx, paragraph ordering and whitespace normalization matter; the evaluator collapses all whitespace with re.sub before comparing, so extra blank lines between merged sections are tolerated.
Open folder/project from terminal using: Check bash history via vm_command_line for presence of 'code ' invocation to confirm terminal was used rather than GUI

Use vscode_config getter with an 'OpenProject'-style extension command that writes the currently open project/folder name to a file, then compare_config with substring/containment check against the expected folder name
Active workspace/project detection: The vscode_config getter triggers a command-palette extension command that dumps the open project path to a temp file on the VM; read that file and check for the expected folder name using substring containment rather than exact match, since full paths vary

Use the 'OpenProject' vscode_extension_command via the command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P) to trigger a custom extension that writes the current open project/folder name to a file, then read that file and check for substring containment of the expected project name.
Python script editing and execution (cod: Use compare_text_file metric to validate script output saved to a file; fetch the result file from the VM and compare stripped text against a gold reference.
When need_rule_judge is true, exact string equality may not be required; consider whitespace normalization options (ignore_blanks, ignore_case) when writing evaluators for similar tasks.
To verify the script was completed and run correctly, check that the output file exists on the VM at the expected path and its content matches the expected program output.
Use compare_text_file metric to validate script output files; fetch VM file and compare stripped text against a gold reference downloaded from cloud storage.

When a script reads instructions from an external document (e.g., docx) and writes results to a text file, verify the output file content exactly matches the expected output using string equality after stripping whitespace.
For algorithm implementation tasks, the output text file captures printed results of running the completed function; ensure the evaluator checks the VM-side output file path, not the source .py file.
Python package installation via terminal: Use vm_command_error getter by running a Python import of the target package; success is indicated by absence of 'Error:' in stderr output.
check_include_exclude on stderr is the standard pattern: include=[] and exclude=['Error:'] confirms a clean import with no ModuleNotFoundError or ImportError.
Package availability can be verified purely via Python import execution without needing to inspect pip list or site-packages directly.
YAML/config file editing: Use yaml.safe_load to parse the saved file and traverse nested keys (e.g., top-level keys and nested dict keys like author.name, author.email) to verify edited values.
check_json with is_yaml=True supports both flat and nested key paths via a list of keys, so verify both top-level and nested fields independently.
When a YAML file has duplicate or aliased keys (common in config templates), safe_load picks the last occurrence; ensure the correct key path is targeted.
File must be saved before retrieval; postconfig Ctrl+S automation is commonly used, so evaluators should account for save timing when reading the file.
Find and Replace in file: Use compare_text_file (exact string equality after strip) against a gold file to verify all occurrences were replaced; fetch the saved file from the VM path after triggering Ctrl+S in postconfig.
When verifying bulk text replacement, read both actual and expected files as plain text and compare full content; no special parser needed — Python open() suffices.

The evaluator saves the file via Ctrl+S in postconfig before fetching, so verification must account for the file being saved post-action; ensure the VM file path matches the edited document's save location.
Extension installation: Use `code --list-extensions` via vm_command_line to enumerate installed extensions; check for the extension's publisher.name identifier (e.g., ms-python.python) using a 'contain' rule on the output string.
Use `code --list-extensions` via VM command line to verify an extension is installed; check that the output contains the expected publisher.extensionName identifier string.
Use `code --list-extensions` via vm_command_line to verify an extension is installed; check that the output contains the expected publisher.extensionname identifier string.
Color theme configuration: Check `workbench.colorTheme` key in `/home/user/.config/Code/User/settings.json` using JSON subset/containment comparison; the `compare_config` metric with `containment_ok=True` parses both JSONs and verifies the expected key-value is present as a subset of the actual config.
Python diagnostics/analysis settings con: VS Code settings are stored as JSON at ~/.config/Code/User/settings.json; use json.load to parse and check nested dict keys like python.analysis.diagnosticSeverityOverrides for exact key-value matches
When verifying nested settings objects, check both the top-level key presence and the inner dict value equality, since a missing sub-key or wrong severity string both yield failure
Debug settings configuration: Parse settings.json as JSON and check for the presence and value of debug-related keys (e.g., debug.*) directly in the top-level object; use json.load and key lookup rather than string matching.
Keyboard shortcut customization (keybind: Read /home/user/.config/Code/User/keybindings.json; handle both standard JSON and files with a leading comment line (skip first line and re-parse if direct json.load fails)

The file contains a JSON array of binding objects; check for presence of a specific dict entry with keys like 'key', 'command', and optionally 'when' — a command prefixed with '-' means removal/unbinding of that shortcut
Use direct list membership check (entry in data) rather than iterating, since dict equality in Python matches all key-value pairs exactly
Read keybindings.json from the VS Code user config path; handle both valid JSON arrays and files with a leading comment line (skip first line then parse)
Check that the keybindings list contains an exact dict entry with the expected 'key', 'command', and optional 'when' fields — use direct membership test (entry in list) rather than substring search
The 'when' clause is a plain string field in the keybinding object; verify its presence and value when context-conditional shortcuts are required (e.g., terminalFocus, editorTextFocus)
Editor word wrap column configuration: Check `editor.wordWrapColumn` key in `/home/user/.config/Code/User/settings.json` using `json.load`; verify the integer value matches the requested column width.
Use `check_json_settings`-style subset matching: iterate expected key-value pairs and confirm each exists with the exact value in the parsed settings dict.
Editor tab wrap configuration: Check settings.json (typically at ~/.config/Code/User/settings.json) by parsing it as JSON and verifying the target workbench/editor key has the expected value; use json.load and direct key lookup.
Save workspace file (.code-workspace): Check for the existence of a `.code-workspace` file at the expected path using a directory listing or file-existence command; the `contain` rule on `ls` output is sufficient since VSCode workspace files have a predictable naming pattern (`<name>.code-workspace`).
Parse the .code-workspace JSON file and check the 'folders' array for expected path entries; paths are stored as relative or absolute strings under the 'path' key in each folder object
Use json.load on the .code-workspace file; the top-level 'folders' key holds a list of dicts—verify both membership and order if required
When folders are added via UI or command palette, paths may be stored relative to the workspace file location, so normalize/compare accordingly
Text indentation editing (indent/outdent: Use compare_text_file (exact string match) to verify indentation changes; read both files and compare stripped content, preserving tab/space characters since indentation is whitespace-sensitive.
When verifying indentation, avoid ignore_blanks mode as it strips tabs and newlines, which would mask indentation errors; use exact comparison instead.
To check indentation programmatically, split file content by lines and inspect leading whitespace characters (tabs vs spaces) per line for the affected range.
Auto-save configuration (files.autoSave: Check settings.json (typically at ~/.config/Code/User/settings.json) by parsing it as JSON and verifying both the autoSave mode key (e.g., 'afterDelay') and the numeric autoSaveDelay key are present with correct types — the delay must be an integer, not a string.
New file creation and save: Use vm_command_line with 'ls' on the target directory and check for filename presence; the 'contain' rule on ls output is sufficient for file existence checks.
File/folder exclude patterns configurati: Parse settings.json as JSON and check that the target key (e.g., 'files.exclude') exists and its value is an object containing the expected glob-pattern keys mapped to boolean true; use json.load and direct dict comparison for nested values.
Multi-root workspace management: To verify multi-root workspace state, inspect the .code-workspace JSON file's 'folders' array or use the accessibility tree to check open editor groups/workspace titles
Python script output verification: For tasks requiring a Python script to print computed results, do not rely only on substring checks for imports, filenames, and print statements; execute the script with vm_command_line and validate stdout, while separately inspecting that it reads the required input file with the requested library.
Python script verification: For tasks requiring a script to read a source file, checking for keywords and expected stdout is not enough; use AST/source checks or behavioral tests to confirm the script actually calls the required library on the target file rather than printing hardcoded values.
vm_command_line script execution: When evaluating scripts saved on the Desktop, run them with cwd set to /home/user/Desktop if Desktop-relative paths would be a reasonable valid implementation.
Python script reading spreadsheet data: For scripts required to read and compute from an input file, AST checks for import/load_workbook plus stdout substrings are not enough; robust evaluators should either run the script against a controlled modified copy of the data or inspect for real workbook/worksheet row or cell traversal and reject hardcoded target strings.
Python script verification for spreadshe: For scripts required to read spreadsheet data, combine AST checks with execution-based checks that discourage hardcoded answers, such as requiring parsed stdout lines with exact expected fields and, when feasible, running against a controlled copy of the workbook or checking code paths that actually consume worksheet values.
vm_command_line versus vm_file getter se: Rule code receiving vm_command_line output should treat result as stdout only; it should not open VM filesystem paths. To inspect a user-created file, use vm_file and open the returned local cached path, or make the command print the file content together with any derived reference data.
code comment audit verification: For tasks asking users to extract values from source-code comments, the evaluator should parse the source file directly to derive both the line numbers and the expected comment-described fixes, then validate the output file exactly rather than using loose substring checks.
plain-text report verification: For tasks requiring a specific line-by-line text format, parse the output as an exact ordered list of required keys and reject extra, missing, duplicate, or out-of-order entries rather than only searching for matching substrings.
source-comment extraction: When the requested answers come from source comments such as '# BUG', the evaluator should parse the sampled source file to derive both the line numbers and the corrected expressions, instead of only checking hardcoded or substring values.
source-comment-derived answers: When verifying answers extracted from source comments, prefer parsing the source file comments dynamically to derive expected line numbers and corrected expressions, rather than relying only on hardcoded expected values.
ground truth command getters: Commands that compute expected repository/file facts should not be scored as independent rule items; otherwise the evaluator can award reward before the user creates the required artifact. Use them as expected data for comparing the submitted output.
multi-rule final artifact scoring: When a task specifies an exact text output format, avoid adding redundant permissive substring rules that can outweigh the strict format rule; instead make one strict rule compare the complete normalized file against dynamically computed expected values.
artifact verification with source-derive: Do not include separate scoring rules that only verify immutable source repository facts; they can produce positive initial reward. Source commands should be expected_getters for checking the user artifact, not independent rewarded result_getters.
vm_command_line getter semantics: vm_command_line returns stdout as a string; rule code should parse that string directly. Only vm_file returns a local cached file path that should be opened.
dependency source files in evaluators: Do not include a scoring rule that checks immutable input/source files from the task setup; it can produce positive initial reward. Use source files only to derive expected values, while scoring should depend on the user-created output artifact.
